stem: A teacher asks the learners in her class two questions and records the answers as two data sets. Data set 1 holds the answers to this question: {=q1} The answers were: "{=d1[0]}"; "{=d1[1]}"; "{=d1[2]}"; "{=d1[3]}". Data set 2 holds the answers to this question: {=q2} The answers were: "{=d2[0]}"; "{=d2[1]}"; "{=d2[2]}"; "{=d2[3]}". Which one of the following correctly categorises the two data sets?

choices.correct: Data set 1 is qualitative {=t1} and data set 2 is qualitative {=t2}.

distractors.text: Both data sets are qualitative anecdotal, because both sets of answers come from the learners themselves.
Both data sets are qualitative categorical, because both are made of words.
Data set 1 is qualitative {=t2} and data set 2 is qualitative {=t1}.

solution: Neither data set can be written as numbers, so both are qualitative.
In data set {=cn} the answers are picked from a limited set of possibilities: only three different answers appear, and some learners gave the same one. So data set {=cn} is categorical.
In data set {=an} each learner answered in a sentence of his or her own, in the form of a story, so data set {=an} is anecdotal.

Both data sets come from the same learners, so where the answers come from cannot tell the two types apart. It is the form of the answers that decides: words picked from a limited set are categorical, and sentences in the learners' own words are anecdotal.
Therefore data set {=cn} is qualitative categorical and data set {=an} is qualitative anecdotal.
notes: Advanced tier: the same learners answer a closed question and an open question, so the student has to separate categorical from anecdotal inside one context and see that who gave the answers does not decide the type (the book's we02 asks for the explanation; ex10-1-1 supplies the anecdotal case). Which question is Question 1 is randomised with flip, so the correct option varies between 'categorical then anecdotal' and 'anecdotal then categorical'; the two 'both' distractors carry the catalogued anecdotal-because-personal and categorical-for-any-words in every instance, and the reversed-order distractor carries no id (it is both mistakes at once, not a catalogued single error). The closed data set always has exactly three different answers, one of them repeated, and both data sets are printed in the same quoted form so the type cannot be read off the typography. Strings are interpolated from lists; the question texts are chosen by conditional expressions, not by concatenation.
